w: Built in stages from 1573 to 1813 - nearly 250 years - directly atop the Aztec sacred precinct beside the Templo Mayor. Architect Claudio de Arciniega drew on Gothic cathedrals back home, and the masons after him layered on Baroque, Churrigueresque and Neoclassical additions as fashions shifted.
s: Built on the holiest ground the Aztecs had
_facts: Built 1573-1813 on the former Aztec sacred precinct near the Templo Mayor, on the north side of the Zocalo
Designed by Claudio de Arciniega, drawing on Gothic cathedrals in Spain
Nearly 250-year construction mixed Gothic, Baroque, Churrigueresque and Neoclassical styles

w: Home to the Aztec Sun Stone and the eerie Xochipilli statue, this is the most-visited museum in the country - 3.7 million people in 2024 alone, enough to rank 17th among art museums worldwide. Opened in 1964 inside Chapultepec Park, though Octavio Paz grumbled its central Mexica hall turned the place into a temple.
s: Mexico's most-visited museum, Sun Stone included
_facts: Holds the Stone of the Sun (Aztec calendar stone) and the Xochipilli statue
Most-visited museum in Mexico: 3,700,000 visitors in 2024, 17th most-visited art museum in the world
Opened 1964 by President Adolfo Lopez Mateos in Chapultepec Park
Octavio Paz criticized the Mexica hall's centrality as turning the museum into a temple

w: Every ruler of this city since the Aztec Empire has kept a palace on this exact spot - much of the current building's material reportedly came from Moctezuma II's original residence. Since 2018 it has doubled as the president's home as well as the seat of Mexico's federal executive, facing the Zocalo.
s: A palace on this spot since the Aztec Empire
_facts: Seat of the federal executive; official presidential residence since 2018
On the Zocalo (Plaza de la Constitucion)
Site has held a palace for Mexico's rulers since the Aztec Empire; built with materials from Moctezuma II's palace

w: Aztec rulers once retreated to this hilltop forest, and 866 hectares of it still function as the city's principal lung. Its oldest section holds the castle, the zoo and the anthropology museum, drawing an estimated 24 million visitors a year - enough to force a major rehab between 2005 and 2010.
s: The city's oldest and biggest green lung
_facts: 866 hectares, considered the first and most important ecological 'lung' of Mexico City
Inhabited/landmark since the pre-Columbian era; Aztec rulers' retreat
First section holds Chapultepec Castle, the zoo and the Anthropology and Tamayo museums
24 million visitors a year; major rehabilitation 2005-2010

w: The shimmering, windowless silver hull in Nuevo Polanco holds 66,000 works spanning 30 centuries - Pre-Hispanic Mesoamerican sculpture beside Rodin, Dali and Tintoretto. Carlos Slim named it for his late wife Soumaya Domit; free entry helped it become Mexico's most-visited art museum by 2013.
s: A silver hull of a museum, and it's free
_facts: Private, non-profit museum with over 66,000 works across 30 centuries
Named for Soumaya Domit, wife of founder Carlos Slim; building designed by son-in-law Fernando Romero's practice fr路ee
Most-visited art museum in Mexico in 2013 (1,095,000 visitors, 56th worldwide); welcomed its five-millionth visitor in 2015

w: Architect Luis Barragan lived and worked behind this deliberately plain 1948 facade until his death in 1988, and the interior still holds his own furniture and private art collection - Picasso and Diego Rivera among it. UNESCO listed it as a World Heritage Site in 2004; tours run by appointment only.
_facts: Former residence and studio of architect Luis Barragan, built 1948, his home until his death in 1988
Retains original furniture and personal art collection including Picasso and Diego Rivera works
Converted to a museum in 1994; named a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2004; visits by appointment

w: Named for the Nahuatl 'hill of the grasshopper,' this is one of only two royal palaces in North America ever inhabited by actual monarchs - Emperor Maximilian and Empress Carlota lived here during the Second Mexican Empire, before it became the National Museum of History in 1939.
s: Where an emperor and a president both lived
_facts: Name means 'on the hill of the grasshopper' in Nahuatl; sacred Aztec site
One of only two royal palaces in North America inhabited by monarchs (with Iturbide Palace) - home to Emperor Maximilian I and Empress Carlota, 1864-67
Served as gunpowder warehouse, military academy and presidential residence (until 1934); National Museum of History since February 1939
